bill.title: the Finish the Arkansas Valley Conduit Act
bill.description: The bill would change how the local share of the Arkansas Valley Conduit is repaid to the federal government. The conduit is a federal drinking-water pipeline for southeastern Colorado. The Bureau of Reclamation, the federal water agency, builds its main pipe. The Secretary of the Interior leads the department that includes Reclamation. The Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District, a local public body, is responsible for repayment. The local share would stay at 35 percent of the pipeline's cost. Money paid during construction by anyone other than the Secretary would count toward that share. If the Secretary found financial hardship, the rest of the share could be repaid over as many as 75 years instead of 50, at half the usual interest rate. The bill would not provide construction money.

claims.title: What H.R.131 changes in the repayment rules
claims.statement: H.R.131 would keep the local share at 35 percent of the conduit's cost and would count money paid during construction by anyone other than the Secretary of the Interior toward that share. Based on a showing of financial hardship, as decided by the Secretary, the remaining balance could be repaid over not more than 75 years, with simple interest at half the rate set under the existing law.
claims.classification_reason: Direct statement of the bill text and of the existing law printed in the committee report. No source in the packet disputes what the text says. Secondary descriptions of a hardship 'forgiveness' option differ from the text and are noted in the scope.
claims.section: H.R.131 (Engrossed in House, July 21, 2025), Sec. 2(1)(B), adding subsection (d)(1) to the first section of Public Law 87-590
claims.source_quote: the contract for the Arkansas Valley Conduit shall provide for payment in an amount equal to 35 percent of the cost of the conduit, notwithstanding the reclamation laws or any other provision of this Act. The contract payments shall consist of-- “(A) funding provided during construction from any entity other than the Secretary; and “(B) based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary, repayment of the balance not covered under subparagraph (A) for a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c), including revenue derived from contracts for the use of excess capacity or exchange contracts using Fryingpan-Arkansas project facilities.
claims.scope_html: The comparison is with the law in force on January 8, 2026. The lower rate and longer period depend on a showing of financial hardship, as decided by the Secretary of the Interior. The text does not use the word forgiveness, although the district's message and one news report describe the hardship clause that way (district newsletter, January 2026; Colorado Sun, January 2026). The bill gives no construction money and does not change the 35 percent share.
claims.background_html:
The Arkansas Valley Conduit is a pipeline planned to carry water from Pueblo Reservoir to 39 communities in southeastern Colorado. The Bureau of Reclamation is the federal agency that builds and manages federal water projects. It is part of the Department of the Interior, which the Secretary of the Interior leads. The Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District is the local public body responsible for repayment.

Existing law provides “100 percent federal construction financing, and 35 percent nonfederal repayment over a 50-year period, starting after project completion” (House committee report). “Nonfederal” here means not paid by the federal government. Repayment must be finished “within fifty years from the time the works are first available for the delivery of water,” with interest based on what the Treasury pays when it borrows (existing law as printed in the committee report). Simple interest means no interest is charged on past interest.
claims.support_html: The bill says the payments shall consist of “funding provided during construction from any entity other than the Secretary” and, “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary, repayment of the balance not covered under subparagraph (A) for a period of not more than 75 years with simple interest at a rate that is equal to 50 percent of the interest rate determined by the Secretary of the Treasury under section 2(c)” (bill text).

claims.title: Easier terms lower the yearly repayment burden on the local side
claims.statement: If hardship is shown, H.R.131's lower interest rate and longer repayment period would lower the yearly amount the local side must find to repay the conduit's construction share, compared with the law in force.
claims.classification_reason: Sourced to the repayment district, Reclamation, the bill's Senate sponsor and the arithmetic of the terms. The veto message objects to who bears the cost; it does not deny that local repayment becomes easier. No point-specific response challenges this step. The limit on reaching household bills is kept in the scope.
claims.scope_html: This concerns the construction share only. The sources do not estimate the change for any household's water bill. The district, not each town, is the repayment body, and revenue from other users of the wider federal water project counts toward the share (district testimony, 2024). Local water systems also pay separately to connect to the conduit and must keep paying for its operation and upkeep (district funding guidance; bill text).
claims.background_html: “Miscellaneous revenues” means money the federal water project earns from contracts with other users, such as contracts to store water in Pueblo Reservoir. These revenues are counted toward the conduit's 35 percent share (district testimony, 2024).
claims.support_html: The district told Congress that after costs rose, miscellaneous revenues would no longer cover the share on the old terms: “Repayment can now be accomplished only if the interest rate is reduced to at least half the current project rate and the repayment period is at least 75 years” (district testimony, 2024). That testimony concerned an earlier bill, but the district said a 75-year period at half the rate would still meet the bill's goals. Senator Bennet says the bill works by “cutting local costs by lowering the interest rate and providing more flexible repayment terms” (Bennet, Senate floor). Reclamation said changes proposed in the earlier bill were “necessary to ensure that the costs of the AVC remain reasonable and affordable for the rural communities that will depend on it” (Reclamation testimony, 2024).

prerequisite_paths.reason: A lower burden follows only from the changed terms and only where hardship is shown.

claims.title: Easier repayment helps the later part of the conduit get built
claims.statement: Compared with the law in force on January 8, 2026, easing repayment under H.R.131 would help the later parts of the conduit get built, and so help more communities receive its water. It would remove one financial obstacle. It would not pay for construction and would not be enough by itself to finish the project.
claims.classification_reason: Directly stated by the president of the district overseeing construction and supported by Reclamation, the House committee chair and a House floor manager. No source in the packet denies it and no point-specific response attacks it. A bill that removes one obstacle can help without paying for the work, so needing other funding limits this claim but does not contradict it. The funding dependence is carried in the scope. This is the most consequential classification choice; the report explains the competing reading.
claims.scope_html:
This claim is about help, not a guarantee. The relief depends on the hardship showing in the bill. The bill “was not an appropriations bill,” so it gives no construction money (district newsletter, January 2026).

Other funding also matters. In May 2025 the district reported federal funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and said the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding” (district newsletter, May 2025). Asked in April 2025 when the project would be finished, a district official said, “That depends on the level of federal funding that we get.” (Colorado Public Radio interview). After President Trump vetoed (rejected) the bill on December 31, 2025, the local water district reported, “Funding already in place was not affected.” (district newsletter, January 2026).

The sources do not explain step by step how the repayment terms change what gets built, and they do not say exactly which work or which places lie in the later part.
claims.background_html: The “trunk line” is the main pipe. Reclamation builds it with federal money. “Spur” and “delivery” lines are smaller pipes that connect communities to the trunk line. The district builds them, using state loans and grants and other non-federal money (district testimony, 2024). An appropriation is money Congress provides for a stated use.
claims.support_html:
After President Trump vetoed (rejected) the bill on December 31, 2025, the local water district's president said: “It’s when we get to the second half of the project where it will be challenging to build and repay our portion of the debt.” He added: “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” (Colorado Sun, January 2026). The law in force also makes a repayment contract “a condition precedent to construction” of these works (existing law as printed in the committee report). A condition precedent is something that must be in place first. The sources do not say this rule is what the district president meant.

The House committee chair said the bill “facilitates the construction of the Arkansas Valley Conduit, or AVC, by easing the repayment requirements for project beneficiaries” (House floor, January 8, 2026). A House member leading the floor debate said the bill would “help finance the project and begin delivering clean, reliable water to rural communities” (House floor, July 21, 2025). Earlier, “the AVC was not constructed with the original project, primarily because AVC beneficiaries were unable to repay all construction costs” (Reclamation testimony, 2024).

prerequisite_paths.reason: The stated route to more construction runs through making the local repayment affordable.

claims.title: Conduit water would be cleaner than current groundwater
claims.statement: Where the conduit is completed, it would replace or add to communities' poor-quality groundwater with filtered water from Pueblo Reservoir, which would remove or reduce the contaminants they now face.
claims.classification_reason: Stated by Reclamation and the repayment district and repeated in the federal environmental review. No source in the packet disputes it and no response challenges it.

arguments.title: Cleaner source water would reduce polluted treatment waste that threatens the Arkansas River and its aquatic life.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Cleaner source water would reduce polluted treatment waste that threatens the Arkansas River and its aquatic life.

  • Because Cleaning local groundwater can create concentrated waste. The local water district told Congress: “When this groundwater is cleaned to drinking water standards, in many cases it produces a reject stream which violates EPA discharge standards.” [3] A reject stream is the polluted water left after treatment.
  • Because La Junta and Las Animas clean their water with reverse osmosis, a filtering process. Their waste reaches the river: “The brine, or salty wastewater, from both towns’ reverse osmosis systems is dumped back into the Arkansas River, creating a new environmental challenge.” [5]
  • Because The waste can carry harmful substances. A 2014 report, discussing possible stricter limits, describes brine “too thick with selenium and other contaminants” [6] and says selenium “becomes damaging to both human and aquatic life at high levels.” [6]
  • Because Conduit water would give Las Animas a source that needs simpler treatment: “The pipeline would deliver clean water straight to the town, requiring only standard treatment like filtration and disinfection.” [5]
  • So Helping communities make this switch reduces the need to produce and discharge polluted waste. Protecting rivers and aquatic life from that pollution serves [NAME]’s care for nature.
arguments.con_html: No response specific to this point is provided.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 provides no construction money. In May 2025 the local water district reported that the Bureau of Reclamation had funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” AVC means the Arkansas Valley Conduit. The trunk line is the main pipe, and Manzanola is a town along the route. Appropriations are money Congress provides. After President Trump vetoed (rejected) the bill on December 31, 2025, the local water district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The local water district's president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and said: “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Here “we” means the district, and “stop” refers to work on the project. Sources: [7], [8], [4].

Evidence note: Rocky Mountain PBS reports that with the money Congress has provided so far, the pipeline would not reach La Junta and Las Animas. Rocky Mountain PBS also reports that La Junta is applying for grants to rehabilitate (repair and update) its water treatment plant and reduce the amount of concentrated waste. It also reports that Las Animas must eventually stop sending this waste into the river. The 2013 federal environmental impact statement (EIS) assumed that under every project option, no liquid waste would be discharged. Brine, the salty waste, would dry up in ponds instead. The EIS also said the present discharge would likely not be allowed to continue. Sources: [5], [9].

Evidence note: The 2013 federal environmental impact statement (EIS) reports 2 acres of permanent disturbance to dry land (upland) for one conduit route, Comanche North. It reports 50 acres for its No Action option, which assumes no conduit. No Action would need ponds to dry brine, the salty waste from expanded reverse osmosis filtering at La Junta and Lamar. The 2013 federal environmental impact statement (EIS) reports about 1,200 acres of temporary disturbance to dry land (upland) under its No Action option, which assumes no conduit. It reports 2,999 to 3,228 acres with the conduit. Disturbed areas are expected to recover within three years. The No Action option in the 2013 federal environmental impact statement (EIS) assumes no conduit at all. That is different from what would happen without H.R.131. Sources: [9].

arguments.title: Operating the conduit would take water out of the river channel and worsen conditions in natural waters.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 4 Operating the conduit would take water out of the river channel and worsen conditions in natural waters.

  • Because The original 2013 review predicts “negligible to minor increases in total dissolved solids concentrations through Pueblo” [9] and “negligible to minor adverse effects on water quality caused by increasing selenium concentrations” [9]. arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: H.R.131 provides no construction money. In May 2025 the local water district reported that the Bureau of Reclamation had funds “enough to construct the AVC Trunk Line to Manzanola by 2030 and design the entire AVC,” and that the completion schedule “will depend on future appropriations or infrastructure funding.” AVC means the Arkansas Valley Conduit. The trunk line is the main pipe, and Manzanola is a town along the route. Appropriations are money Congress provides. After President Trump vetoed (rejected) the bill on December 31, 2025, the local water district reported that “Funding already in place was not affected.” The local water district's president said repayment becomes challenging in “the second half of the project” and said: “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” Here “we” means the district, and “stop” refers to work on the project. An acre-foot is the water needed to cover one acre one foot deep. That is about 2 percent of the average yearly flow at the river gauge above Pueblo. arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 H.R.131 would use shared public resources for added financing relief while vulnerable families elsewhere still lack affordable water.

  • Because Existing law bases interest on what the Treasury pays to borrow money: “the computed average interest rate payable by the Treasury upon its outstanding marketable public obligations” [2].
  • Because Financing federal water projects costs the government money. A federal audit agency explains: “These funds are borrowed from the U.S. Treasury and accrue interest until repaid.” [16]
  • So The bill charges half that rate on the same unpaid balance and lets public financing last longer. Taxpayers cover more of the cost of lending.
  • Because Later repayment also has a cost. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the budget office of Congress, explains that an amount received “today is more valuable than the same amount received or paid in the future.” [17]
  • Because CBO lists an “Increase” [18] in direct spending of less than “$500K” [18] for the amended bill.
  • Because Other water needs remain unmet. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reports that “the need for both capital investment and operations support still outpaces the tools at utilities’ disposal.” [19]
  • Because Those needs affect families' protection and opportunities: “High water bills can force families to cut back on other essential expenses, such as food, healthcare, and education.” [19]
  • So Public money used to cover this added financing help cannot also meet other needs. Protecting vulnerable people gives [NAME] a reason to oppose having taxpayers cover these added costs while families elsewhere struggle to afford basic necessities.

With the May, 2024, updated cost estimate, this is no longer true.” [20] Miscellaneous revenues means money from contracts with other users of the federal water project.

arguments.title: Helping construction continue would put Native cultural ties to ancestral places and burial traditions at risk.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Helping construction continue would put Native cultural ties to ancestral places and burial traditions at risk.

  • Because Current financing creates a stopping point. Water district board president Bill Long explains the bill's importance: “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” [8]
  • Because The project's 2022 federal review identifies prehistoric sites in the area it could affect: “Archaeological resources also include two prehistoric sites.” [9]
  • Because The review also records a tie to living tribes: “PA consulting parties, including all invited Indian Tribes, are as follows” [9], a list that includes the “Comanche Nation” [9]. A PA, or programmatic agreement, is the plan for handling historic places.
  • Because The review treats finding undisturbed historic places as a construction risk. Its route plan aims “to diminish the probability of encountering any undisturbed historic properties.” [9]
  • Because The review does not guarantee avoiding every burial: “All known burials or cemeteries will be avoided to the extent possible.” [9] It also plans for a burial that “cannot be avoided or is encountered during construction” [9], including under the federal Native American graves law on federal or trust land.
  • So Easing the financial barrier helps more construction go forward with a remaining risk to ancestral places and graves.
  • Because These places matter to living cultures. The National Association of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers explains: “Connections to cultural heritage sustain the health and vitality of Native peoples.” [10]
  • Because Disturbing graves can violate the beliefs expressed through burial traditions. Southern Ute preservation official Cassandra Atencio explains: “When you put somebody in the ground, you expect them to stay there because you made prayers or did something over them, and that meant something so they could go somewhere else. When you uncover that, you're disturbing them, and now you're bringing them back.” [11]
  • Because Listening to and accepting people with different beliefs gives weight to their cultural ties and burial practices, even when [NAME] does not share those beliefs.
  • So Respecting those practices gives [NAME] a reason to oppose financing that advances this risk of disturbance.
  • Note This argument concerns disturbance itself. The plan requires compliance before work restarts: “only when compliance has been completed.” [9] That cannot undo any disturbance that led to discovering a grave.

arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 Helping replace contaminated water would protect against cancer, kidney harm and infections.

  • Because Communities the conduit would serve have unsafe water sources: “The drinking water sources they rely on are often contaminated with unsafe levels of radium, uranium, and other pollutants.” [5]
  • Because These radioactive substances raise cancer risk: “Exposure to radionuclides from drinking water results in the increased risk of cancer.” [6] The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) also identifies uranium's danger to the kidneys: “toxic effects to the kidney” [6].
  • Because Some groundwater is affected by surface water that “contains harmful microorganisms and pollutants.” [7] Microorganisms are germs too small to see.

  • Because Local water providers would disinfect the delivered water before it enters household water systems: “AVC Project Participants would be responsible for adding a disinfectant residual (likely free chlorine) at the entry points to their distribution systems.” [7]
  • Because Disinfection protects water on its way to the tap: “This remaining disinfectant kills germs living in the pipes between the water treatment plant and your tap.” [9]
  • So Easier financing helps complete a safer water source, with local disinfection. That reduces cancer, kidney and infection risks for people who drink this water, including any ordinary American living, working or staying in these communities. arguments.pro_html:

  • Because The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, the federal water agency, found groundwater with “cancer-causing radioactive contaminants including naturally occurring radium and uranium.” [5]

  • Because The finished conduit will deliver clean water to “39 rural communities across southeastern Colorado.” [6]
  • Because Protecting shared drinking water serves societal security. The federal plan for water security calls the water sector “a lifeline sector” [7] and states: “Safe drinking water is a prerequisite for protecting public health and all human activity” [7].
  • So Helping finish a shared safe-water system strengthens the government's ability to defend U.S. communities against a documented health threat. That serves [NAME]'s concern for a country that protects its citizens.

Evidence note: H.R.131 provides no construction money. After President Trump vetoed (rejected) the bill on December 31, 2025, the local water district reported that funding already in place was not affected and that construction continued. The Colorado Sun and Water Education Colorado report that remaining funds would pay for about three to five more years of construction. arguments.title: The added financing cost would draw on federal resources available for defense and emergencies.
arguments.pro_html:
Point 1 The added financing cost would draw on federal resources available for defense and emergencies.

  • Because The existing interest rate is tied to what the Treasury pays to borrow: “computed average interest rate payable by the Treasury upon its outstanding marketable public obligations” [1].
  • Because Getting the same payment later is worth less. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO), the budget office of Congress, explains that “an amount received or paid today is more valuable than the same amount received or paid in the future.” [19]
  • Because CBO's July 2025 table lists the bill's effect on direct spending as “Increase by Less Than $500K” [20].
  • So The cheaper financing adds a federal cost. Keeping the current terms preserves the federal resources that cover it.
  • Because Federal financing costs compete with defense spending. A report by the chair of Congress's Joint Economic Committee states: “Interest costs use revenue that could be used for other government outlays, such as national defense.” [21]
  • Because CBO identifies “respond to unforeseen events” [22] as another purpose of federal tax and spending policy.
  • Because [NAME] values a state with the means to defend its citizens and protect them against new threats.
  • So Preserving money available for defense and emergency action serves that value and gives [NAME] a reason to oppose this added financing help.
arguments.con_html:
Response The argument treats higher promised repayments as money that keeping the current terms would preserve. The record reports a payment problem under those terms. This response does not dispute that CBO lists a small direct-spending increase, and it does not answer the argument's reasoning from a federal cost to resources for other uses.

  • Because The bill makes the easier repayment terms depend on hardship: “based on a demonstration of financial hardship, as determined by the Secretary” [2].
  • Because In 2024 testimony on an earlier bill, the repayment district judged whether income from contracts to use project facilities could cover its share after construction costs rose: “Repayment can now be accomplished only if the interest rate is reduced to at least half the current project rate and the repayment period is at least 75 years, 25 years longer than the currently authorized 50 years.” [23]
  • Because Reclamation, the federal water agency, confirmed the payment problem under the existing law: “Given this increase, the project beneficiaries are again faced with challenges to repay their share of construction of the project, as directed under P.L. 111-11.” [10]
  • Because The argument's own CBO source says, as a general method, that CBO counts missed payments when valuing loans. It describes “the expected cost of default, which CBO accounts for in projected cash flows rather than in the discount rate.” [19]
  • So An interest rate tied to federal borrowing costs and an earlier due date set what is owed. They do not show what would be collected. Comparing the value of the promised payments leaves out the payment problem. The argument has not shown that keeping the old terms preserves the higher repayments it counts as available money.
arguments.notes_html:
Evidence note: Later accounts by others describe the bill’s hardship rule differently from the bill’s text. The local water district’s message after the veto says the bill “Provides an opportunity for a federal decision on debt forgiveness based on economic hardship,” and the Colorado Sun says the bill may have allowed the Bureau of Reclamation to forgive some loan payments. The bill text allows a repayment period of up to 75 years at half the Treasury rate only with a demonstration of financial hardship. It does not use the word forgiveness. Sources: [8], [15], [2].

Evidence note: The only cost figure for H.R.131 in these sources is a July 2025 listing by the Congressional Budget Office (CBO): “Increase by Less Than $500K” in direct spending and no effect on revenues. CBO says the table was prepared with limited review time. Sponsors say the bill “does not authorize any additional Federal funding.” The statements cited from Congress's Joint Economic Committee (JEC) and the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) concern the national debt in general. HR131_C02.support: The district told Congress that after costs rose, miscellaneous revenues would no longer cover the share on the old terms: “Repayment can now be accomplished only if the interest rate is reduced to at least half the current project rate and the repayment period is at least 75 years” (district testimony, 2024). That testimony concerned an earlier bill, but the district said a 75-year period at half the rate would still meet the bill's goals. Senator Bennet says the bill works by “cutting local costs by lowering the interest rate and providing more flexible repayment terms” (Bennet, Senate floor). Reclamation said changes proposed in the earlier bill were “necessary to ensure that the costs of the AVC remain reasonable and affordable for the rural communities that will depend on it” (Reclamation testimony, 2024).

HR131_C03.support:
After President Trump vetoed (rejected) the bill on December 31, 2025, the local water district's president said: “It’s when we get to the second half of the project where it will be challenging to build and repay our portion of the debt.” He added: “Without this legislation there will be a point where we will have to stop.” (Colorado Sun, January 2026). The law in force also makes a repayment contract “a condition precedent to construction” of these works (existing law as printed in the committee report). A condition precedent is something that must be in place first. The sources do not say this rule is what the district president meant.

The House committee chair said the bill “facilitates the construction of the Arkansas Valley Conduit, or AVC, by easing the repayment requirements for project beneficiaries” (House floor, January 8, 2026). A House member leading the floor debate said the bill would “help finance the project and begin delivering clean, reliable water to rural communities” (House floor, July 21, 2025). Earlier, “the AVC was not constructed with the original project, primarily because AVC beneficiaries were unable to repay all construction costs” (Reclamation testimony, 2024).

HR131_C04.support: Reclamation says: “The AVC will eliminate or reduce the effects of those contaminants by delivering filtered water from Pueblo Reservoir.” (Reclamation news release, 2022). The district says: “The AVC will provide a new surface water source of high quality” (district testimony, 2024). The 2022 review says the water is needed to “supplement or replace existing poor-quality groundwater sources” (2022 environmental assessment).

HR131_C05.support: A January 2026 House speech says: “The drinking water sources they rely on are often contaminated with unsafe levels of radium, uranium, and other pollutants.” (House floor, January 8, 2026). Reclamation found groundwater with “cancer-causing radioactive contaminants including naturally occurring radium and uranium” (2014 record of decision). EPA says: “Exposure to radionuclides from drinking water results in the increased risk of cancer.” It also identifies “damage to the kidneys from exposure to the uranium itself” (EPA fact sheet).

HR131_C06.support: Reclamation says “total dissolved solids have corrosion and scaling effects that lead to premature deterioration of distribution pipes, water treatment equipment, and household appliances” (2014 record of decision). The 2022 review keeps the benefit of “reducing total dissolved solids concentrations in AVC Project Participants’ water supplies” (2022 environmental assessment).

HR131_C07.support: “The brine, or salty wastewater, from both towns’ reverse osmosis systems is dumped back into the Arkansas River, creating a new environmental challenge.” (Rocky Mountain PBS, 2026). The pipeline “would deliver clean water straight to the town, requiring only standard treatment like filtration and disinfection.” (Rocky Mountain PBS, 2026). The district's president said: “And the only way to correct the discharge problem is to have a cleaner source of water.” (Rocky Mountain PBS, 2026). The Colorado Sun refers to “the Arkansas River’s own water quality problems, which can be worsened by the discharges.” (Colorado Sun, October 2025).

HR131_C08.support: Treating contaminants “forces many families to rely on bottled water or expensive filtration systems to meet basic needs that we all take for granted” (House floor, January 8, 2026). The 2022 review says communities “increasingly face expensive alternative remedies such as reverse-osmosis, ion exchange, filtration, and bottled water” (2022 environmental assessment). State notices can tell customers to use “filter systems or buying drinking water and not drinking the water that's coming out of the taps” (Colorado Public Radio interview).

HR131_C09.support: Communities “continue to face unreliable water supplies and serious water quality challenges” (House floor, January 8, 2026). A district official says: “The pipeline is needed to make sure that the supply of water is steady.” (Colorado Public Radio interview). Local “springs that supply some of the underground water sources can dry up periodically” (Municipal Sewer & Water, 2025). Reclamation warns that without a realistic option, “these same communities would be unlikely to achieve sustainable water treatment” (Reclamation testimony, 2024). Reclamation also says the conduit “will help meet existing and future municipal and industrial water demands” (2014 record of decision).

HR131_C10.support: Senators Hickenlooper and Bennet write: “The completion of the Arkansas Valley Conduit would mean water for rural schools in communities such as Lamar, which are teaching the next generation. It would mean water for hospitals in towns such as La Junta, which are keeping Coloradans healthy.” (MS NOW opinion article, January 2026).

HR131_C11.support: The district reports that “the median household income is only $47,000 as compared to the Colorado median household income of $89,000” (district testimony, 2024). Median means the middle household. Reclamation says “families and communities across the Lower Arkansas Valley face rising water treatment costs in a declining local economy” (Reclamation testimony, 2024). The project plan calls it “an economically challenged area of rural Colorado” (project plan, 2020). A district official cited the region's “low income, and its shrinking population and economy” (Colorado Sun, October 2025).

HR131_C12.support: The federal review says: “A control plan for fugitive dust would be developed and implemented to minimize particulate and dust emissions during earth work.” (2013 environmental impact statement). The decision record calls for measures “to minimize particulate and dust emissions from the construction site” (2014 record of decision). Fugitive dust means dust that escapes into the open air.

HR131_C13.support:
The usual rate rests on “the computed average interest rate payable by the Treasury upon its outstanding marketable public obligations” (existing law as printed in the committee report). The bill would charge half of that on the unpaid balance. CBO explains that “an amount received or paid today is more valuable than the same amount received or paid in the future” (CBO report on discount rates). CBO's table lists the bill's effect on direct spending as “Increase by Less Than $500K” (CBO table, July 2025). The veto message says the bill would be “forcing Federal taxpayers to bear even more of the massive costs” (veto message, December 2025).

On the other side, the bill's sponsor says it “does not authorize any additional Federal funding” (House floor, January 8, 2026), and Senator Bennet says it “costs the American taxpayer nothing” (Bennet, Senate floor).
HR131_C13.response:
This claim counts the higher payments under the old terms as money the government would keep. The district responsible for repayment says expected project revenues no longer cover those terms: “When Public Law 111-11 was enacted, miscellaneous revenues were expected to be more than sufficient to repay 35 percent of the AVC’s cost with interest and within 50 years. With the May, 2024, updated cost estimate, this is no longer true.” (district testimony, 2024). Reclamation also says “the project beneficiaries are again faced with challenges to repay their share of construction of the project” (Reclamation testimony, 2024).

So the amount owed under the old terms does not show the amount that would be collected. CBO's general method also counts expected missed payments when it values loans (CBO report on discount rates). This objection does not show that the cost is zero. CBO's table still lists an increase, and no source says what the old terms would really bring in.
